⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I think about luxury vehicles, the first things that instantly come to mind are $60,000+ price tags.
  • It has been revealed that each of them has a distinct take on the "sensibly priced" formula, delivering upscale tech, all-wheel drive, and genuine everyday utility without drifting into absurd price territory.
  • With an as-tested price of $44,250, it undercuts the $51,790 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro by a wide margin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I think about luxury vehicles, the first things that instantly come to mind are $60,000+ price tags. Thankfully, entry-level luxury crossovers exist, and they’re some of the smartest buys on the market. For my next comparison, I’m pitting the Mini Countryman and Audi Q3 against each other in a head-to-head matchup to see which compact crossover is worth buying.

It has been revealed that each of them has a distinct take on the "sensibly priced" formula, delivering upscale tech, all-wheel drive, and genuine everyday utility without drifting into absurd price territory. It’s actually been years since I last tested a Mini — the electric Countryman EV — so you can imagine how eager I was to get back into the gas-powered 2027 Mini Countryman S All4.

With an as-tested price of $44,250, it undercuts the $51,790 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro by a wide margin. I will say, however, that you can’t dismiss the Q3 just yet, because after a week’s worth of driving, it too impressed me on plenty of occasions.

2.0L TFSI turbocharged I4 Engine.

2.0-Liter MINI TwinPower Turbo Inline 4-Cylinder Engine.

22 mpg city / 29 mpg highway / 25 mpg combined.

24 mpg city / 32 mpg highway / 27 mpg combined.

Frankly, this one’s tough because these compact crossovers cater to completely different tastes, so personal preference heavily influences the decision.

The 2026 Audi Q3 leans heavily into conventional luxury aesthetics, dressed in Malpelo Blue Metallic with the Black Optic package — which shimmers in the light. Alongside the sharp LED headlights up front and OLED taillights in the back, the package makes it look sleek and unmistakably upscale.

It has been revealed that by contrast, the 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 embraces a sportier edge and distinctive British flair. It’s undeniably boxier and more upright, yet it’s loaded with personality — I especially love its Slate Blue Metallic paint job with a contrasting black roof and stripes. Even its LED lighting features customizable light signatures to match its charming looks.

Ultimately, it comes down to whether you prefer understated German luxury or retro-modern charm — making this category an easy tie.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Best short distance fuel economy.

Best long distance fuel economy.

Looking at their spec sheets, it’s quite clear that the 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 holds a slight advantage in terms of fuel economy with an EPA-estimated 27 mpg combined (24 city / 32 highway), compared to the 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro’s 25 mpg combined rating (22 city / 29 highway).

It has been revealed that in my real-world testing, however, that gap turned into a surprisingly wide canyon. Over 313.6 miles of mixed driving in the Countryman, I averaged an impressive 31.1 mpg overall — easily exceeding its EPA estimate. Better yet, it hit 30.5 mpg on my best short-distance trip and soared to 36.1 mpg on a longer highway stretch.

Sources indicate that in contrast, the Audi Q3 struggled to match its window sticker across 243.5 miles of testing, averaging just 23.2 mpg overall. Even on my best long-distance (26.5 mpg) run, it never came close to its 29 mpg highway rating.

If keeping fuel costs low is a top priority, the Mini is the clear standout here, saving you noticeably more at the pump in the long run.

Most compact crossovers prioritize fuel economy and put driving dynamics in the back seat, but not these two. Better yet, I love how both prove you don’t need a massive engine to have fun behind the wheel.

It has been revealed that the 2027 Mini Countryman S All4 is my favorite of the two by a narrow margin, packing a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four engine that puts out 241 horsepower and 295 lb-ft of torque. The Audi similarly has impressive muscle under the hood: a 2.0-liter TFSI four-cylinder that delivers 255 horsepower and 273 lb-ft of torque.

What I will say after being behind the wheel of both is that they’re noticeably zippy off the line, with speedy acceleration that makes it effortless to overtake at cruising speed. While the Q3’s powertrain actually surprised me with a smooth delivery that almost makes it feel more like an EV, it doesn’t beat the Countryman when the road starts to curve. The Mini's lower, wider stance keeps it feeling noticeably more planted through corners, preserving that signature go-kart agility it’s known for.

Despite their smaller footprints, these compact crossovers still offer plenty of room to make lengthy road trips a breeze. However, the 2027 Mini Countryman S All4 holds a slight advantage. That’s because it offers 40.4 inches of front legroom and 37 inches in the rear, which beats the 2026 Audi Q3’s 40 inches up front and 36.1 inches in the back. Additionally, they deliver nearly identical trunk space around 25 cubic feet, easily accommodating my electric scooter.

Industry observers note that inside, they take very different approaches to cabin materials. The Audi leans into traditional luxury with genuine leather seating surfaces, wood inlays, and solid soundproofing that keeps road noise at a minimum. Obviously, the higher price of the Q3 is justified by its more luxurious aesthetics.

Sources indicate that mini takes a totally different approach that gives it a charming style that feels genuinely original. It trades classic leather for Vescin leather-free upholstery and knitted textile surfaces on the dash and doors — which I have to say looked funky and stylish at first glance, but they eventually grew on me.

Sure, the Audi comes up a smidge short on rear legroom, but the Q3 just feels noticeably more plush over long stretches. And when I factor in Audi’s smoother, more intuitive adaptive cruise assist on highways, the Q3 edges ahead as the more relaxing cruiser.

Audi needs to prove it’s worth spending about $7,500 more over its rival. But does it?

According to recent reports, while the 2026 Audi Q3 doesn’t skimp on luxury amenities, it simply makes you pay noticeably more for them. Even so, I appreciate its crisp 360-degree camera coverage, head-up display that projects driving details onto the windshield to lessen distractions, and seamless Park Assist Plus for automatic parking. Inside, its panoramic sunroof and vibrant LED ambient lighting create a more upscale look at night — while its large blind-spot warning lights mounted right on the side mirrors are impossible to miss in heavy traffic or in the daytime.

According to recent reports, however, you’re still getting better value for the money out of the Mini Countryman S ALL4. For starters, its circular 9.4-inch OLED touchscreen display is a sight to behold and runs a far more intuitive interface. Although it ditches the traditional driver’s cluster entirely, the flip-up head-up display keeps distractions at a minimum. I’m also major on sound, and the punchy Harman Kardon surround sound system easily outclasses the Audi's Sonos setup.

Industry observers note that not only does it offer full 360-degree camera coverage, but it also includes a clever Backup Assistant that takes over the wheel and automatically retraces the path I took to get into the spot. And finally, I really love the adaptive LED headlights with customizable light signatures and cornering lights.

When I weigh this robust feature set against that $7,540 price gap, the Mini delivers far more bang for your buck.

Recent findings suggest that let me finish by saying that I’d gladly buy either compact crossover in a heartbeat with my own money. That noted, the 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro does come up short once the tallies are counted.

It has been revealed that if you prioritize traditional luxury materials, a quieter cabin, and a smoother adaptive cruise control system for long highway commutes, it remains an immensely likable daily driver that costs less than the average luxury vehicle. Honestly, despite losing this head-to-head matchup, I would still gladly buy the Audi Q3 — it’s just that the Mini Countryman gives you more for less.

The 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 emerges as the clear winner, and it’s the one I’d ultimately pick. Between its punchy driving dynamics, standout real-world fuel economy, sharper OLED infotainment system, and $7,540 price advantage in this comparison, it simply delivers too much personality and value to ignore.

Latest Update: How to clear slippery moss and green algae from patio pavers — without blasting out the sand

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Damp, shady weather turns even the best-kept patio into a slippery green mess, and reaching for a pressure washer is not always the smartest fix.
  • Fortunately, you do not need heavy machinery to get your patio looking clean and safe underfoot again.
  • It has been revealed that while a power washer strips surface grime in minutes, it only removes the visible top layer of moss and algae, leaving microscopic spores behind in the pores of the stone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Damp, shady weather turns even the best-kept patio into a slippery green mess, and reaching for a pressure washer is not always the smartest fix. High-pressure jets can blast jointing sand straight out from between your pavers, pit soft natural stone, and leave behind micro-scratches where moss and algae grow back even faster.

Fortunately, you do not need heavy machinery to get your patio looking clean and safe underfoot again. A stiff broom, a watering can, and a few simple household staples or outdoor treatments are all it takes to lift stubborn green growth without damaging your stonework.

It has been revealed that while a power washer strips surface grime in minutes, it only removes the visible top layer of moss and algae, leaving microscopic spores behind in the pores of the stone. Worse still, blasting delicate limestone, sandstone, or older mortar joints with high-pressure water erodes the surface and loosens the pavers themselves.

Gentle cleaning methods work differently. Instead of relying on brute force, they break down the organic growth at the root so you can brush or rinse it away cleanly, keeping both your stone surface and the sand between your pavers intact.

Before applying any cleaner, move patio furniture out of the way, sweep away loose leaves with a stiff broom (avoid metal rakes, which can scratch pavers), and lightly water any nearby lawn or flowerbeds so plants do not absorb soapy or acidic runoff.

Once prepped, choose the method that best suits your patio material:.

If you have delicate natural stone like limestone or sandstone, or simply want the gentlest fix, start with a bucket of warm water and a few generous squeezes of dish soap.

According to recent reports, pour the sudsy mixture over the pavers, let it sit for 15 minutes to loosen the grime, and scrub diagonally across the joints with a stiff outdoor brush so you do not dislodge the sand. Rinse thoroughly with a garden hose.

For heavier green buildup on concrete or brick pavers, wet the patio down first, scatter washing soda crystals (sodium carbonate) across the affected areas, and add a small drizzle of dish soap.

Work the paste into the pavers with a stiff brush, then leave it to sit for 24 to 48 hours before hosing it away. Always wear gloves when handling soda crystals, and keep pets off the patio until it is rinsed clean.

Skip this method on natural stone: because vinegar is acidic, it can etch and discolor limestone, sandstone, or travertine.

Mix equal parts white vinegar and water in a watering can or garden sprayer, saturate the mossy patches, and leave the solution to soak for 20 to 30 minutes before scrubbing with a stiff brush and rinsing well.

Recent findings suggest that if you are tackling a large patio or stubborn black-spot lichen, an oxygen- or enzyme-based outdoor paver cleaner saves hours of scrubbing. Apply the solution with a watering can on a dry day, leave it to break down the spores over a few days, and let the next rainfall wash the dead growth away naturally.

  • Issued November 20, 2026  |  Last updated November 23, 2026 (UTC).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 20, 2026 by GL.iNet.

SECURITY NOTICE · CUSTOMER ADVISORY.

GL.iNet Router and KVM Security Incident.

Issued November 20, 2026  |  Last updated November 23, 2026 (UTC).

On November 20, 2026, GL.iNet identified a vulnerability in its cloud remote management services. An unauthorized party exploited the vulnerability to access and install malicious software on some GL.iNet routers and KVM devices.

The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident. Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. The cloud-side fix alone does not remove malware from devices that were already infected; install the security firmware below to remove it.

Industry observers note that install the latest stable security firmware for your exact model as soon as possible, even if the checks below find no signs of infection. The security firmware update removes the malware identified in this incident without requiring a factory reset. You can keep your existing settings during the update.

If your router is not listed, check the GL.iNet Download Center or email support@gl-inet.com. Do not install firmware for another model. An unlisted model is not necessarily unaffected.

If you installed a security beta, upgrade to the latest stable firmware for your model.

Follow the steps below to check your device. For both routers and KVM devices, look for the exact text crond -i /tmp/.log within the details of a running process. The process entry may contain other information.

According to recent reports, sign in to your router via SSH and run the following command. If you are unfamiliar with SSH, please refer to our Router SSH Login Guide or contact our technical support team at support@gl-inet.com for assistance.

In the KVM web interface, go to Toolbox → Terminal → Access to open the device terminal. For step-by-step instructions on Comet Q (RMQ1), see the KVM Console Guide. Run the command for your model in the KVM’s terminal, not on the connected computer.

According to recent reports, as a precaution, check for unfamiliar programs, browser extensions or user accounts; unexpected startup items or scheduled tasks; and unusual settings changes or network activity. Run a full scan with up-to-date security software.

Sources indicate that as our investigation continues, additional indicators of compromise have been identified. The official quick checks described above may not detect every affected device.

Industry observers note that both checking approaches are available for GL.iNet routers and KVM devices: the official device-specific quick checks above and the optional third-party tool below. Follow the instructions appropriate for your device. The two approaches have different detection coverage, and neither can guarantee that a device is free of compromise.

For people who wish to perform a more comprehensive check, an independently developed community tool is available:.

Community Security Check Tool (Unofficial).

According to recent reports, disclaimer: This is an independent third-party tool and is not developed, verified, maintained, endorsed, or supported by GL.iNet. GL.iNet does not control the tool's functionality, accuracy, security, availability, or data-handling practices, and cannot guarantee its results. Use of this tool is entirely optional and at the user's own discretion and risk. It is not part of GL.iNet's official support or remediation process.

It has been revealed that before using the tool, review its instructions and source code. It may run with administrative privileges and includes optional remediation, evidence-collection, and reporting functions. Owners should evaluate those functions carefully before enabling them. The absence of findings does not guarantee that a device has never been compromised.

For official device recovery instructions and security firmware updates, please continue to follow GL.iNet's published guidance.

For questions, please contact support@gl-inet.com.

To report a security problem, contact security@gl-inet.com.

We apologize for the concern this may cause and are committed to keeping you informed.

Founded in 2010, GL.iNet is a leading provider of innovative routers and networking solutions. From compact travel routers to cutting-edge remote KVMs, GL.iNet delivers award-winning networking technology designed for performance and security.

In a recent development, GL.iNet gives people and organizations the power to connect with confidence. By putting control in the hands of users, GL.iNet supports the productivity and collaboration that shape a Good Life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27.3 is right now in beta testing with developers and public beta customers. The update includes multiple newly introduced features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 ….

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

As my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone users sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:.

So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

The redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final patch.

According to recent reports, the redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 users, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

According to recent reports, for Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a new Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

Sources indicate that for iPhone Duo users, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left, making it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

Industry observers note that reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

iOS 27.3 also brings a new face unlock feature to iPhone Duo. This is not full-fledged Face ID. Instead, Apple is using the front-facing camera on the iPhone Duo’s outer display to recognize you, then unlock the device. It doesn’t work for things like Apple Pay and passwords.

iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

Sources indicate that finally, iOS 27.3 includes a new option in the Settings app to have your iPhone Duo lock when closed. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold it, rather than transition content from the inner display to the outer display.

When it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with fresh clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

In a recent development, this includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The update also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

Sources indicate that iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the patch expands Siri AI with many newly introduced capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:.

We started rolling out these fresh capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

Industry observers note that there are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

With iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test new ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:.

Industry observers note that today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple states it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to upcoming languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

iOS 27.3 also introduces usage limits on select Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features. The limits apply to things like:.

According to recent reports, you can unlock higher usage limits with an eligible iCloud+ plan, starting at $2.99 per month. If you hit your usage limit, basic Siri requests will still work. That includes things like setting timers and alarms.

iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:.

Sources indicate that iOS 27.3 is a major update to Safari. First, the update adds support for a fresh vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

Recent findings suggest that iOS 27.3 also adds a new Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

For Apple Music consumers, iOS 27.3 adds a fresh “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

The upgrade also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

There are two key changes to the Apple TV app in iOS 27.3. First, the update introduces video podcasts in the TV app. You can now watch your favorite video podcasts in the TV app, and sync your playback progress between the TV app and the Podcasts app.

Recent findings suggest that second, iOS 27.3 adds vertical video to the TV app. The app now includes a new “Explore Clip Collections” section where you can browse clips from Apple TV content in a TikTok-style design.

Here are a few other changes in iOS 27.3:.

This is the biggest percentage discount I've come across on a Garmin right now, and it makes the Instinct 3 AMOLED very tempting as a reliable adventure watch that offers incredible battery life and a distinctive look.

This is perhaps the best deal going on a Garmin right now. It's on of five Garmin deals I've been looking out for this Black Friday, because even though the Forerunner 265 is an older watch, it's still an excellent multisport tracker with a bright AMOLED display, and it even comes in two sizes.

The Vivoactive 6 is a slick-looking smartwatch with impressive sports tracking credentials, as you'd expect from a Garmin. It has dropped as low as $229 in the past though, so a better deal might be yet to come on the watch this Black Friday.

The Forerunner 965 is the best value alternative to newer top models like the Forerunner 970 and even the Fenix line-up. It packs brilliant sports tracking and navigation features into its slim, attractive case, and you'll be hard pressed to find a better watch from any brand for $449.

The Garmin Venu 4 combines the good looks of a smartwatch with Garmin's excellent sports tracking, and even as a marathoner I prefer it to the more sports-focused Forerunner 570, partly because it has a built-in flashlight.

Even at this reduced price I don't think the Forerunner 570 offers better value than the Venu 4 or Forerunner 965, but it does have some more striking design options than those watches, which might swing it for some. It's still a great sports tracker of course, but lacks maps and a flashlight, which is a shame.

It has been revealed that the Venu X1 is a bit of an oddity in the Garmin line-up, with its ultra-thin design and short battery life, but it's actually packed with the same brilliant sports and navigation features as you get on the Forerunner 970. At $300 off, it might be the sleeper hit.

If you want the cheapest good alternative to the Fenix 9 Pro, then right now it's the Epix Pro thanks to this deal. However, the Epix Pro has dropped to just $499 in the past, and I still have hope we'll see that price again this Black Friday.

Industry observers note that the best overall sports watch on the market, the Forerunner 970 is still expensive even when reduced by $100, but it's well worth its price. It has a sleek, attractive design and all of Garmin's flagship features aside from LTE connectivity.

In a recent development, while this is a good price for a great adventure watch, the fact that the Fenix 7 Pro has been superseded by three rounds of Fenixes at this point makes me hope there might still be better deals to come on it and the Epix Pro. If not, this is still worth looking at as the cheapest titanium Garmin watch with maps and a MIP display in the sales.

Having just tested the Garmin Enduro 4, I'd say the Enduro 3 is the better value buy for sure, because it has all the same key features as the upcoming watch for $200 less in the sales. Those features include the best battery life of any Garmin, thanks the Enduro 4's MIP display and solar panels.

The Fenix 8 is one of my favorite Garmins of all time, partly because the orange color is absolutely gorgeous. Unless you need the connectivity features on newer Fenix models, I'd say the Fenix 8 is also a better value option in sales right now, because it's not missing much else that you do get on the Fenix 8 Pro and Fenix 9 Pro.

It has been revealed that massive savings are available on the Fenix 8 Pro line-up right now, with Black Friday following close on the heels of the launch of the Fenix 9 Pro. The new watch has a few upgrades, including an all-titanium case, but the Fenix 8 Pro is certainly a savvier buy thanks to this $350 saving in my opinion.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It premiered quietly on Netflix back in February, earned glowing reviews, and then more or less vanished, skipped by audiences and passed over for a second season despite being one of the smartest things the streamer put out all year.
  • If you’re ready for a wickedly funny mystery that’ll have you laughing one minute and gut-punched the next, keep reading.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, too many murder mysteries telegraph their twists a mile away. This scrappy little series takes a familiar setup and pushes it somewhere much weirder and funnier than you’d expect. Three women in their late 30s reunite for the funeral of a childhood friend, only to start suspecting her death was no accident. That’s how “How to Get to Heaven from Belfast” opens — and it might just be the funniest, most underrated show most people never bothered to watch this year.

It premiered quietly on Netflix back in February, earned glowing reviews, and then more or less vanished, skipped by audiences and passed over for a second season despite being one of the smartest things the streamer put out all year. The show comes from Lisa McGee, the creator of the beloved “Derry Girls,” though you shouldn't walk in expecting more Catholic-schoolgirl hijinks. This is a darker, twistier beast: a genuine murder mystery that happens to be laugh-out-loud funny, trading teenage chaos for middle-aged mayhem. Across eight tightly wound episodes, McGee’s razor-sharp writing and a trio of electric lead performances turn a simple whodunit into a story about grief, friendship, and the secrets we bury—all set to a killer ’90s soundtrack.

If you’re ready for a wickedly funny mystery that’ll have you laughing one minute and gut-punched the next, keep reading.

Sources indicate that saoirse (Roisin Gallagher), Robyn (Sinéad Keenan), and Dara (Caoilfhionn Dunne) were inseparable as teenagers in Belfast, part of a tight-knit group of four. Now in their late 30s, they’ve drifted apart and moved on with their lives — until the sudden death of the fourth member of their group, Greta, brings them back together for her funeral.

What should be a simple reunion swiftly spirals into something a lot weirder. The women start to suspect that Greta’s death wasn’t the accident everyone’s calling it. In fact, it may tie directly to a secret from their shared past, one they’ve spent years trying to forget.

Determined to find out what really happened, the trio rolls out an investigation that takes them well beyond Belfast — even landing them at a resort in Portugal — as the past they’ve been outrunning finally catches up with them.

In a recent development, I’ll keep this simple: The show is funny, the mystery is sharp and the two actually work in tandem. Most of the credit goes to Lisa McGee’s writing. She pulled off the same balancing act on “Derry Girls,” where the comedy never undercut the emotional gut-punches. Doing it again here with older characters and darker stakes makes the show feel far more grounded than most mysteries in its lane.

According to recent reports, roisin Gallagher, Sinéad Keenan, and Caoilfhionn Dunne play women who’ve known each other since childhood, and you buy it immediately. They bicker, cover for each other, and slip back into old habits the way real lifelong friends do. Their chemistry is electric—and given how much time they spent together on set, it’s easy to believe that bond carried over off-camera.

In a recent development, best of all, it’s a self-contained eight-episode miniseries, meaning the whole story is here and it actually has an ending—no cliffhangers. You can knock it out in a weekend without worrying about Netflix abruptly pulling the plug on a resolution.

It didn’t get nearly the attention it deserved the first time around, which is exactly why it’s worth seeking out now. If you want a smart, funny mystery you can start and finish without a massive commitment, it’s streaming on Netflix — so make sure to catch it (and “Derry Girls” too, if you haven't already).

Stream "How to Get to Heaven from Belfast" on Netflix.

#73911. Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (937 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple.
  • Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….
  • Macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple. Interestingly, it appears to have been coined by the company’s customers and then used by reviewers before it was later picked up by Steve Jobs.

Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….

Macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing. It was subsequently used by a number of reviewers. The earliest example I can find of Steve Jobs adopting it was in 1999, when discussing the rollout of FireWire to the Mac in the PowerMac G3.

It has been revealed that it’s hot-pluggable. You don’t have to turn your computer off to connect and disconnect peripherals, you can just plug them right in. Again, the drivers are dynamically loaded. There are no terminators and there are no switches. It just works.

(If you have a link to any earlier example, please do let me know in the comments.).

I’m a massive fan of the philosophy. Most of the time, users should just be able to get on with the tasks they want to execute without having to worry about the technology. The tech that makes it all possible should sit there quietly in the background.

However, there are cases where I think Apple takes this approach a little too far, and where tech-savvy people at least would like a little more transparency and control.

AirPods firmware updates are a good example. Back in September, there was quite a significant patch in the form of custom EQ. It’s a rather basic version, but still a feature many had wanted for a long time. Instead of being able to manually trigger the update, consumers had to wait until it “just worked.”.

Apple’s support document has a how-to guide that is essentially an outline of the conditions required to permit an patch, and an instruction to simply wait until it happens. Which you will only know by repeatedly checking.

Sources indicate that make sure your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Connect your charging case to a power source. Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to be updated. Check the firmware version again.

In a recent development, another example, and one I’ve complained about before, is that there is no way to manually trigger an iCloud document sync, nor any progress indicator when it does finally happen. In the best of cases, it takes seconds; in the worst, many hours. And again, the only way to find out is to repeatedly check.

It’s the same story when shooting a video on your iPhone. Will it still be there an hour later, available to instantly edit and view? Maybe, or maybe it will have been offloaded to the cloud, requiring it to be downloaded before you can do anything with it – while a video you shot months earlier is still stored locally on the device! You can, of course, switch off optimization altogether, but if you choose to use it, you get no control over it. I want a setting that allows me to do things like specify local retention of all photos and videos taken within the past fortnight.

According to recent reports, will that video be available in the Mac Photos app when you check half an hour later? Maybe, maybe not. You can click the Sync Now button as many times as you like, and it will apparently have no effect, claiming it’s up to date despite the video being entirely absent. It will be there when it’s there.

Once it is in the Photos app on your Mac, it’s a similar story when exporting it to a folder. You can drag and drop the video into the folder, and this time you are manually triggering the transfer (yay!), but there will be absolutely no visual indication that it is in progress. No grayed-out icon, no progress bar, nothing. So far as the user interface is concerned, it appears that your drag and drop had no effect – until the video file finally appears.

I think with all of these things and more, Apple needs to offer options. Yes, most non-tech users may be perfectly happy to just wait until things happen, but there ought to be a standard way to trigger things that presently happen in their own sweet time, as well as progress indicators and confirmation that a process is complete.

Industry observers note that is this an ecosystem-wide improvement you’d like to see? Please share your thoughts in the comments and add any frustrating examples of your own.

#73909. Breaking: Expert reveals 7 common bedroom items that can trigger 3 a.m. wake ups — here’s what to remove from your bedroom to start sleeping through the night

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2107 w)

Breaking: Expert reveals 7 common bedroom items that can trigger 3 a.m. wake ups — here’s what to remove from your bedroom to start sleeping through the night

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that here at Tom's Guide, we know that nighttime wake-ups are a big issue for many people.
  • You might not realize it, but elements of your sleep space could be contributing to your disrupted rest — from technology and light usage, to elements of your bed itself.
  • With advice from two sleep experts, we're exploring why bedroom environment matters, what to consider changing and why those adjustments are important for sleep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that here at Tom's Guide, we know that nighttime wake-ups are a big issue for many people. Which is why, if you've found yourself repeatedly awake at 3 a.m. and unable to fall back to sleep, it's time to take a look around your bedroom.

You might not realize it, but elements of your sleep space could be contributing to your disrupted rest — from technology and light usage, to elements of your bed itself. The simple act of removing them might be the difference between another broken night's rest and staying asleep all night.

With advice from two sleep experts, we're exploring why bedroom environment matters, what to consider changing and why those adjustments are important for sleep.

Recent findings suggest that temperature, light and sound pollution can all stop you from staying asleep all night."People sleep better when it's dark, when it's quiet, when it's cool, when it's free of disturbances [and] when it's safe, states Dr. Aric Prather, sleep scientist and expert at UCSF and BetterSleep. "And so, trying to optimize that environment on those facets, is certainly a step towards a better night of sleep.".

In a recent development, while 3 a.m. wake ups have a variety of causes, there are environmental factors that can contribute to them happening, and keep you awake. Here, we explain what they are, and how removing certain items from your room can help.

Both experts we spoke to advised, where possible, to keep work outside of the bedroom. And since many of us work on computers or laptops at home, removing these from your sleep space can help eliminate distracting light sources and potential stress they're associated with.

According to recent reports, the Sleep Foundation points out that having electronics near the bed can contribute to nighttime wakeups through the noise and light they can emit. So, we asked Heather Darwall-Smith, a UKCP psychotherapist specializing in sleep and author of The Science of Sleep, if laptops in the bedroom can be impactful on sleep, through the association with work or light from charging cables.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In a recent development, if it's your work laptop and it's near your bed and you see the light [this can prompt], 'Oh, that's my work laptop. Oh, God, did I send that email?'.

According to recent reports, "It's both," she states. "The mind needs to know the day is done. It's like putting work away. It's creating that boundary between work and home," she explains.

Dr. Prather also points out that waking and seeing a light from a laptop charging cable can carry anxiety. "Because if it's your work laptop and it's near your bed and you see the light [this can prompt], 'Oh, that's my work laptop. Oh, God, did I send that email?'" he indicates, adding that it can also lead to ruminating over the next day being a work day.

He adds that "some people's computers have fans that are constantly running and there's heat coming out of them. So that can change the the temperature of the room or the temperature near their body.".

As temperatures drop over the winter, keeping your heating on overnight can appear to be a sensible way to combat the seasonal chill — but being mindful of temperature is key to avoiding waking up.

“High temperatures in your bedroom can interfere with your body’s natural cooling process, which is essential for falling and staying asleep,” Dr. Hannah Patel previously explained.

In a recent development, but turning your heating off in the lead-up to bedtime — ideally anytime from around 9 p.m. (though that's not a hard and fast rule if you're an early bird or a night owl!) — you'll allow your bedroom time to cool down.

Similarly, sleeping with an electric blanket is another nighttime practice to be particularly careful with.

Not only is it unsafe to keep an electric blanket on all night (the Electrical Safety Foundation International says they should never be used while sleeping), even modern models with built-in protection to prevent overheating, advise turning off before falling asleep.

Removing your phone from the bedroom is something the Tom's Guide sleep team swears by, in part because expert advice suggests that scrolling your phone late at night can cause a state of mental arousal that may lead to disrupted sleep.

Industry observers note that not to mention, a recent study found that every hour spent on screens before bedtime increases the risk of insomnia by a whopping 59%. As Dr. Prather points out, "phones on their own aren't really problematic, but if people can't keep their hands off them, then they are.".

And while the jury is still out on how much blue light from screens is really going to affect your sleep, looking through your phone in the middle of the night can stimulate your brain and prolong awakenings.

However, Darwall-Smith notes that she often finds "people are more stressed by taking the phone out of the bedroom than having it there.".

If that's you, consider "turning off your notifications, thinking about how checking the screen or getting into live activity on your phone is going to keep you awake," the sleep psychotherapist advises.

It's the literal foundation of your sleep, but you might not have considered that your mattress could be playing a significant part in disrupting it.

Waking up with back pain or stiffness, aching shoulders and hips, overheating during the night, tossing and turning, and even waking up coughing and sneezing can all be signs that your mattress is the culprit behind your nighttime wake ups.

"If you're constantly having back pain or your mattress isn't okay... look into it," states Darwall-Smith, though she points out that back pain might be caused by factors outside of your mattress.

Industry observers note that dr. Prather suggests finding a mattress that is "the right comfort for you, and that probably changes as you age," and recommends "one that supports your posture [and] that doesn't cause pain.".

Sources indicate that however, as Darwall-Smith notes, "sometimes it's not in [people's] control to change their mattress. So what can you do to make the mattress comfortable? You might want a topper." The best mattress toppers can adjust the comfort and feel of your mattress, and even help with regulating the temperature, all without the cost involved in replacing your existing bed.

Having the wrong pillow for your sleep position, one that has lost it's shape and support, is aggravating allergies or is causing neck pain can all contribute to nighttime wakeups.

Research indicates a relationship between an uncomfortable pillow and poor sleep. One study looking at pillow performance found that everyone "who reported poor sleep quality also reported poor pillow comfort.".

Sheets, meanwhile, might be something of an afterthought, but synthetic fabrics can trap heat and cause sweaty wake-ups — even though the often low price-point can seem attractive.

In a recent development, dr. Prather indicates that along with the right mattress, "the quality of the sheets," and their "breathability" as well as "the quality of the pillow, can all contribute to how comfortable people are, and certainly comfort is something that we want to foster when we're trying to get people to sleep well.".

Our best pillows of 2026 can help you determine what's right for you and our guide to the best bed sheets sets of the year has options for different sleep preferences, seasons, and budgets.

While a basic alarm clock can be a better option that relying on your phone, if it's visible from your bed it's potentially making nighttime wakeups worse.

According to recent reports, "I prefer people to use actual alarm clocks and to try and find non-alarming alarm clocks," says Darwall-Smith. However, she adds that "I prefer people not to look at their clock.".

According to research, clock-watching or 'time monitoring behaviour' (TMB) is common in people who experience insomnia, and something that perpetuates the symptoms of the condition.

Looking at the clock when you wake during the night is "only bad news" says Dr. Prather. "I deal with people with insomnia, but most people are looking at the clock hoping that it's later in the night than it is. And they're almost always wrong.".

Being aware that it's not as late as you hoped then leads to "an immediate anxiety or frustration or discouragement, which pushes against falling back asleep," he explains.

Obviously, we're not suggesting getting rid of the main light in your bedroom altogether, and living each evening in a state of complete darkness.

It has been revealed that but if you find yourself awake during the night? "You should not turn on significant lights," states Dr. Prather. "If you can keep it low light, that's certainly better.".

Speaking of light at night, Darwall-Smith explains that "if you're shining light into your brain at 4 a.m., that's not [good]. Because sleep is reset by the light-dark cycle. As we push towards wakefulness, our eyes register light and it's part of what pushes us up into [being] awake.".

However, Dr. Prather cautions against "[sitting] in the dark with your thoughts, usually that isn't a good solution." He recommends activities that are sleep supportive, relaxing and distracting, like reading with a book light, or using a Kindle on low intensity.

Being wide awake in the middle of the night is rarely pleasant, but you don't always have to be concerned by a brief awakening.

Recent findings suggest that "Waking up during the night is normal... it's part of sleep structure. Especially as people get older, it would be very uncommon for people to not wake up during the middle of the night," claims Dr. Prather.

Perfectionism is insomnia's best friend.

Darwall-Smith agrees, adding that, "What we're looking at is the quality of what that waking is. If you get up, wander around, go and have a pee, go back to bed, happy days. You get up and your eyes are peeled to the ceiling and you're freaking out, not so happy days.".

Recent findings suggest that and though we've covered ways you can help your sleep by adjusting your bedroom environment, the experts we spoke to emphasized focusing on what works for you, and not adding stress by focusing on creating a 'perfect' environment. "We're not looking for perfection. We're looking for good enough to sleep better," indicates Dr. Prather.

It has been revealed that darwall-Smith agrees: "Perfectionism is insomnia's best friend. And if we're rushing around trying to perfect our sleeping conditions, Well, do we really need to? Good enough is good enough.".

We've talked about what to remove, but there are useful products which can help tackle issues with noise, light and comfort that may be impacting your night's rest. You don't need to strive for absolute perfection, consider these as tools for a calmer, more relaxing night. Even better, these three items are all reduced in the Black Friday mattress deals.

It has been revealed that in our Ozlo Sleepbuds 2 review we awarded these tiny buds with 4 starts, with our lead tester noting that she "hoped they would drown out noise so I could stay asleep all night. And they do." Right now, you can get a pair for $40 off in Ozlo's Black Friday & Cyber Monday Sale.

In a recent development, this Sabrina Carpenter approved sleep mask is made with 100% mulberry silk and promises total blackout for a night free from light pollution. It's also adjustable to suit everyone, and the wraparound silk means it's soft on your skin and hair. Plus, it has 30% off in the Amazon Black Friday sale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I’ve used Apple’s Calendar app for years, and there’s an elegant simplicity to it. But one key area the app has long lagged behind competitors is event creation.

When you need to create a latest event, the Calendar app historically has required manually filling in various fields for the title, date, time, invitees, etc. By contrast, the excellent third-party app Fantastical lets you type in natural language and it automatically fills in relevant parameters based on what you type.

In iOS 27, Apple finally introduces its own natural language input for Calendar events. You can type out your event details and certain recognized parameters will be used to automatically fill in the detail fields.

While the feature still isn’t on par with what Fantastical offers, since it doesn’t support as many data points as the third-party alternative, it’s very much a step in the right direction.

Apple has always pitched Siri as being like a personal assistant. As such, calendar-related tasks should have been Siri’s strong suit. But until iOS 27, you couldn’t actually manage your calendar very well using Siri.

With Siri AI, that’s changed in a massive way. Now, you can do things like:.

Sources indicate that one of my favorite personal examples is from this summer when the NFL schedule was released. I asked Siri to find the Dallas Cowboys schedule and add every game to my calendar, and it pulled this off with ease.

Siri is so much better than before at assisting with your calendar, and iOS 27.3 will bring even more capabilities soon.

According to recent reports, what are your favorite iOS 27 Apple Calendar upgrades? Let us know in the comments.

#73903. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3559 w)

Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • Recent findings suggest that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

Recent findings suggest that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

It has been revealed that “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell notes. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

The screen highlights my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

Recent findings suggest that for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

According to recent reports, but can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” notes Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

It has been revealed that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

In a recent development, yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

According to recent reports, sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team revealed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Recent findings suggest that remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

It has been revealed that I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

It has been revealed that this system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

In a recent development, sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

It has been revealed that about a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga notes. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In Latest York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

Industry observers note that in the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

Industry observers note that “The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Sources indicate that surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson notes. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

It has been revealed that after preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

Industry observers note that in 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Sources indicate that absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Sources indicate that noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga indicates.

Sources indicate that still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more key than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell claims. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” claims neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

Recent findings suggest that but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

Recent findings suggest that and connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu claims.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

According to recent reports, telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra states. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

In a recent development, if smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

Industry observers note that in September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Industry observers note that neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

Sources indicate that in the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell claims. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

According to recent reports, the procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as promptly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell indicates. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

According to recent reports, A few months after my visit, Remedy unveiled US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Recent findings suggest that sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he claims. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

Industry observers note that the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this newly introduced technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

According to recent reports, these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person manufacturer into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

💡 Key Takeaways
