📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the iPhone 18 Pro Max isn't the only 18 Pro Max to be released this year, now that Xiaomi has just revealed the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max flagships. The two phones share more than just a name, though, and it seems Xiaomi has adopted a very Apple-looking camera bump on the back of its phones. But considering the camera specs are totally different, I started wondering what the actual quality differences were.

Recent findings suggest that the iPhone 18 Pro Max is one of the best camera phones, sporting a trio of 48MP camera lenses: one main, with variable aperture, an ultrawide angle, and a telephoto lens with 4x optical zoom. The zooming camera offers up to 16x "optical quality" and has a maximum magnification of 40x. The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, on the other hand, has a 200MP main lens, a 50MP ultrawide and a 200MP telephoto with 3.2x optical zoom.

You'd think that the higher resolution camera would produce the best photos, right? Well we've seen time and again that resolution doesn't always equal quality, especially now that camera phones rely on software just as much as they do hardware. That's why phones like the iPhone 18 Pro Max perform so well in our photo shootouts.

In a recent development, but obviously the only way to find out for sure is to actually take some photos and compare the results from each phone. So, out of iPhone 18 Pro Max and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, which 18 Pro Max actually has the best cameras?

The latest and best iPhone, the iPhone 18 Pro Max comes with a new variable aperture camera, a larger battery, incredible performance from the A20 Pro chipset and all those other things that make the iPhone worth owning.

While not officially available in the U.S., the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max has a lot of great features. They include a rear-mounted display, 200MP main and telephoto camera lenses, a 6.98-inch display with Privacy Display and an enormous 7,050 mAh battery.

Sources indicate that the main camera shot is quite different on both phones. The Xiaomi certainly excels in taking a brighter photo, but the result means that the lighter areas look considerably more washed out compared to the iPhone. The overall quality isn't as good either, since the iPhone can pick up more detail in the surroundings, such as my dogs' fur and the gravel on the path. In contrast, the Xiaomi tends to blur those finer details together, especially in the background.

Shooting indoors, things are a little more balanced, but it's clear that the Xiaomi's camera isn't quite as focused as the iPhone's, and most of the Lego set is blurry in comparison to Apple's camera. However the coloring and detail seem to be much closer than they were with the outdoor shot.

The Xiaomi camera's habit of brightening up the image seems to work in its favor on the ultrawide angle lens, with the iPhone adopting a more washed out and drab-looking color temperature. There are reasons for that, and it all comes down to Apple's automatic white balance being somewhat anti-Fall.

However, coloring aside, the detail on the iPhone-captured shot just isn't there. You can even see it in the grass if you look closely, with all the stalks looking pixelated and blurred, compared to the much sharper detail captured by the Xiaomi.

Sources indicate that when it comes to color, the Xiaomi does edge the top spot with slightly more vivid coloring of these berries, in part thanks to the slightly brighter images. The iPhone hasn't washed out the coloring in this instance, and manages to offer a nice bright image with solid contrast between the different colors.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's front camera sports a 50MP sensor, compared to the 18MP one on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, but how much of a difference does it make? As was the case with the rear cameras, the photo is a lot brighter, which really highlights the fact that the sun is shining directly onto my face. Meanwhile the iPhone's shot is a little darker, but the tones seem more true to life and don't make it look like this is my first time outside in several months.

According to recent reports, the quality is good on both, even going so far as to pick up the reflection of my other dog in my sunglasses. However, zooming in reveals how much of a difference high resolution can make. Xiaomi's rendition of my reflected dog is clear and almost perfect, while the iPhone's is pixelated and grainy. Then again, the rest of the photo is fine, and zooming right in isn't something a lot of folks will be doing.

Xiaomi's Portrait mode is, honestly, incredibly disappointing. The bokeh effect is barely noticeable, and it doesn't really emphasize myself in the same way that the iPhone does. The IPhone 18 Pro Max ramped up that effect to the point where the background isn't that visible, and it makes me pop out a little more. The quality of the photo isn't quite as good, but with the extra bokeh and the return more accurate coloring, it's the clear winner.

Industry observers note that zooming into 4x magnification and things are fairly even. The iPhone's coloring is a little more drab than Xiaomi's, but the overall quality of the zoomed-in shot is basically the same, to the point where it's more about personal preference than anything else.

Jumping up to 8x magnification and you can see how Apple's "optical quality" feature really shines. The shot of my dog at this magnification is much more clear than that of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, which noticeably merges the finer details of my dog's fur. The contrasting colors on the Xiaomi's telephoto is more noticeable than the iPhone's, but the loss of quality really lets the team down.

In a recent development, if you increase the magnification to 40x, there's absolutely no question about which camera is better. It's Xiaomi's, simply because the phone produced a clear and crisp shot that the iPhone just can't compete with. I assume some AI upscaling was involved, as is the case with so many other phones, and it's something that Apple consistently fails at. Maybe that's something Apple can include on the iPhone 20.

According to recent reports, going right in with the Macro mode, and the iPhone takes the crown once again. As with before, the picture isn't as bright as Xiaomi's shot, but that doesn't actually matter in this case. The iPhone managed to produce a much crisper photo, with bright colors and details that Xiaomi's camera didn't quite match.

In a recent development, low light performance can make or break a camera phone, and I'm honestly a little torn over which camera is better in this situation. The iPhone 18 Pro Max produced a shot that is brighter and captured more detail, but it also appears somewhat overexposed in the process.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max managed to capture less detail on the church and its surroundings, despite the higher resolution camera, but produced a shot that looks slightly nicer — so long as you don't zoom in too much. And, honestly, I can't tell you which one I like better.

Sources indicate that overall, the iPhone 18 Pro Max managed to beat out the Xiaomi in more categories, though, the two phones drew in several rounds. That shows that Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's camera is no slouch, but not enough to beat the iPhone's camera in those core categories. The quality of the 8x zoom in particular was especially disappointing, since a 200MP lens should have the resolution to be able to cut down a high-quality image to simulate extra magnification — just like Apple does.

Given the choice, and purely based on camera performance, I'd pick the iPhone 18 Pro Max over the Xiaomi. Still the iPhone 18 Pro Max didn't dominate, and the Xiaomi camera certainly manages to produce some great shots. The fact they tied in four different categories just goes to show that these two phones are both very capable camera phones.

But Xiaomi obviously needs to work on fixing its shortcomings, including capturing more detail in low light, improving the bokeh effect and all those other things that could make the camera even better.

Popular secure messaging app Signal has rolled out a new update that automatically disables screenshots for the sake of blocking Siri AI from reading your chats. Here are the details.

Signal’s latest app update on iPhone disables a key system feature: taking screenshots.

As Signal told Reuters, that’s because Apple doesn’t presently provide better tools for iOS developers to safeguard app content from Siri AI and third-party AI agents.

By default, consumers who update and try to take a screenshot will see a message that states: “Screenshot prevented by ‘Block Siri AI’ setting.”.

Fortunately, there’s an easy workaround. Users who want to re-enable screenshots can do so by visiting Signal’s privacy settings and turning off the new toggle that’s labeled ‘Block Siri AI.’.

Here’s 9to5Mac’s own Arin Waichulis:.

Signal now blocks in-app screenshots on iPhone to keep Siri AI from reading chatsIt’s a new toggle in settings that’s on by default, but can be turned offNo equivalent for its Mac app pic.twitter.com/ImsinqMNPq.

Here’s exactly what that toggle does, per the in-app settings:.

Recent findings suggest that prevent Siri AI from scanning Signal content. This will also block you from taking screenshots in the app and App Switcher.

It’s good to see that owners can manually disable the latest privacy setting if they want. But Signal’s decision to block screenshots does raise notable questions about the potential gap in privacy tools for iOS developers.

Apple already lets you block Siri AI from accessing whichever apps you manually exclude, and that became even easier in iOS 27.2. But rather than directing consumers to that system option, Signal seems to believe it needed to take action itself with this upgrade.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places.
  • This shift changes how devices are designed.
  • This White Paper explains these challenges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

And that sprawling library isn't just about quantity, but quality, too, with content from major film studios including Paramount, MGM and Lionsgate, and television networks including A&E, Lifetime, and Starz.

But to keep that platform feeling fresh and interesting, every once in a while Tubi has to say goodbye to some fan-favorite flicks and series to make room for a new wave of film and TV titles. And with another month rapidly coming to a close (where exactly did November go?), that means you'll have to act promptly if you want to catch these three great movies for $0 before they're gone.

Whether you're in the mood for a weepy autumnal favorite, a beloved Ben Stiller comedy, or a little dystopian trip back to Panem, here are three movies to stream before they leave Tubi soon.

According to recent reports, ben Stiller, Robert De Niro, Blythe Danner, and Teri Polo are all back for a fourth "Meet the Parents" movie, "Focker in Law" — with the added fun of Ariana Grande playing a Focker daughter-in-law — which hits theaters nationwide on November 25. If you want to go back to the beginnings of the comedy franchise, though, the original "Meet the Parents" movie is available to watch on Tubi, but not for long.

If you missed the 2000 comedy all those years ago, "Meet the Parents" stars Stiller as the unfortunately-named Greg Focker, who is desperate to impress the parents of his girlfriend (Polo) during her sister's wedding, a goal made significantly more complicated by the fact that her dad is a formidable and overprotective CIA agent (De Niro).

Stream "Meet the Parents" on Tubi now.

Grab the Kleenex: It's "Stepmom" season. The foliage-filled 1998 weeper stars a Golden Globe-nominated Susan Sarandon as Jackie Harrison, a divorced mother of two who's been diagnosed with terminal cancer. As she battles her illness, she must contend with her ex-husband's fresh partner, the much younger and career-driven Isabel Kelly (Julia Roberts), who will soon become the stepmother of Jackie's beloved children, Anna (Jena Malone) and Ben (Liam Aiken).

Though critics at the time dinged the tearjerker for its melodrama ("Solid work from Julia Roberts and Susan Sarandon isn't enough to save 'Stepmom' from a story whose manipulations dilute the effectiveness of a potentially affecting drama," reads the critical consensus on Rotten Tomatoes), "Stepmom" has become an enduring fall favorite thanks to its cozy, family-focused vibes and those iconic leading ladies.

In case you somehow haven't heard, there's a big new "Hunger Games" movie in theaters today: "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," which centers on the 50th Hunger Games, about a quarter-century before Katniss Everdeen's participation.

Stream "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" on Tubi now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27 gives the Messages app a variety of welcome upgrades, including one I’ve found myself using a lot: a Smart Reply feature that’s now personalized to the user’s writing style.

When the first wave of Apple Intelligence features were announced in 2024, one that I immediately thought sounded useful was Smart Reply.

The idea behind Smart Reply is simple. Rather than needing to manually type out replies in Messages and Mail, your iPhone can offer prewritten replies you can choose and send with a couple taps.

Great in theory, but the ‘Smart’ part of Smart Reply struggled to materialize in iOS 18.

Sources indicate that fortunately, with a key Apple Intelligence upgrade in iOS 27, the new version of the feature finally lives up to its name. Per Apple:.

Smart Reply in Mail and Messages can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.

Recent findings suggest that before, Smart Reply would look at the context of a conversation to craft its suggestions. But now, it also aims to match your writing style, punctuation, and tone.

Sources indicate that in iOS 18, I almost never used Smart Reply. That’s because despite being fine at suggesting replies that technically worked, those suggestions didn’t sound like me at all.

Industry observers note that that’s changed in iOS 27. Smart Reply now consistently impresses me. It no longer offers generic responses that sound like AI wrote them. Instead, its suggestions actually fit with my normal style of communication.

Recent findings suggest that the only drawback is that right now, you’ll only ever see two Smart Reply suggestions. If Apple expanded the feature by letting you scroll horizontally through more options, I suspect I’d use Smart Reply even more.

Have you been using iOS 27’s Smart Reply feature in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

HomeKit Weekly: Lafaer’s 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes an annoying automation in Apple Home

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home.
  • HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.
  • A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home. The only carve-out is lighting, because some rooms are hard to judge by time of day alone. Depending on the windows and placement against the sun, some rooms might need light-based automations earlier in the day than others. The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes that with a light sensor most motion sensors lack, along with mmWave radar.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations. If you’re still for long periods, you’re invisible, and the automation assumes the room is empty. The Lafaer LWR02 pairs PIR with 2.4 GHz mmWave radar. The PIR-based motion sees you walking in, and the radar sees the minor stuff, like breathing and shifting on the couch, so the room stays “occupied” for as long as you are in it. The two together also reduce false positives from ceiling fans, curtains, and the dog, because the radar and PIR both must agree before the sensor reports motion.

In Apple Home, that shows up as an occupancy sensor and a motion sensor from the same device.

Sources indicate that “Turn on the lights when someone enters” is a common automation I use, but it can be tricky. What if you only want it when it’s not light outside? Doing it based on time of day sometimes works, but what about depending on where the windows are facing, etc.? You might have a room that gets darker an hour earlier than another room. “Turn on the lights when someone enters, and it’s dark in the room” is what the light sensor can handle for you.

In a recent development, in the Home app, that means triggering a sensor for occupancy, then converting the automation into a Shortcut and adding a condition for the light level. It’s a few extra steps, but it does really give you more fine control over how it works.

Presence, motion, light, temperature, and humidity all come from the same device, and each one appears in Apple Home as its own sensor, so you can build automations around whichever ones fit the room.

According to recent reports, it’s IPX3-rated, so bathrooms, kitchens, and laundry rooms are fine to use in. Coverage is about 13 feet for presence and 26 for motion across about 120 degrees, which works in a bedroom, office, or bathroom. It’s not going to cover a great room from one corner. The base is a magnetic half sphere, so you can aim it, and it mounts with adhesive or sits on a shelf. I generally like to use the shelf for these types of sensors.

The Lafaer LWR02 is Matter over Thread, so it pairs directly with a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K with no Lafaer hub or account needed. It runs on two included AAA batteries, is rated for up to two years, and rechargeable AAAs work with it as well. Thread is why a sensor doing this much can last that long on batteries. All sensor data is processed locally, so it only uses a trickle on the batteries.

It has been revealed that lights that turn off while you’re sitting still in the room are the reason a lot of people stop using motion automations in smart homes. The Lafaer LWR02 fixes that with mmWave radar and then lets you have more granular control of light-based automations based on what’s actually in the environment in the room, not just the time of day.

The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor is available on Amazon.

#73890. A Partial Evaluator for C

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 34m • 📚 Deep Dive (6774 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Labri ↗ Open Full Page

A Partial Evaluator for C

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 34 min read (6774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Labri

⏱️ ~34 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Partial evaluation is program transformation that automates a program specialization process.
  • It has been revealed that tempo is an off-line specializer; it is divided into two phases: analysis and specialization.
  • In a recent development, following the analysis phase, the specialization phase generates a specialized program based on the annotated program and the values of the known inputs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What is Tempo? Partial evaluation is program transformation that automates a program specialization process. Tempo is a partial evaluator for C programs. It has been applied in various domains such as operating systems and networking, computer graphics, scientific computation, software engineering and domain specific languages. A first workshop on Tempo has been organized in March 1998. Tempo is now being distributed. Its documentation is available on line, as well as tutorial slides. An Overview of Tempo Tempo is a partial evaluator for C programs. It is being developed in the Compose project at IRISA / INRIA - LABRI (France). Tempo is an off-line specializer; it is divided into two phases: analysis and specialization. The input to the analysis phase consists of a program and a description of which inputs will be known during specialization and which will be unknown. Based on this knowledge, dependency analyses propagate information about known and unknown values throughout the code and produce an annotated program, indicating how each program construct should be transformed during specialization. Because C is an imperative language including pointers, the analysis phase performs alias and side-effect analyses in addition to binding-time analyses. The accuracy of these analyses is targeted towards keeping track of known values across procedures, data structures, and pointers. Following the analysis phase, the specialization phase generates a specialized program based on the annotated program and the values of the known inputs. Tempo can specialize programs at compile time (i.e., source-to-source tranformation) as well as run time (i.e., run-time binary code generation). For more details, please consider reading some of our papers, most of which are available at the following URL: papers. Program Analysis As a first step, the user provides a program and specifies what arguments (including global variables) are static. For example, the user provides the following code for a miniprintf function, and specifies in this way that the first argument is static whereas the second is dynamic: miniprintf(S,D). miniprintf(char fmt[], int val[]) {   int i = 0;   while( *fmt != '\0' ) {     if( *fmt != '%' )        putchar(*fmt);     else       switch(*++fmt) {         case 'd' : putint(val[i++]); break;                      case '%' : putchar('%');     break;         default  : prterror(*fmt);   break;       }     fmt++;   } } From this Tempo produces a program file with analysis annotations. These annotations can be visualized using colors that highlight the propagation of the known/unknown information throughout the program. /*  LEGEND:  STATIC  DYNAMIC  */ miniprintf(char fmt[], int val[]) {   int i = 0;   while( *fmt != '\0' ) {     if( *fmt != '%' )        putchar(*fmt);     else       switch(*++fmt) {         case 'd' : putint(val[i++]); break;                       case '%' : putchar('%');     break;         default  : prterror(*fmt);   break;       }     fmt++;   } } The blue color (bold face for black and white display) represent static constructions, i.e. values that can be computed at specialization time. The red color (standard font for black and white display) is for dynamic expressions, whose value cannot be precomputed knowing only the static arguments. Basically, everything in blue (bold) will disappear after specialization; only red (standard font) parts will remain. The visualization of the analysis is very important for the user to assess the amount of specialization in the code. Furthermore, the analysis speeds up the specialization process (as opposed to on-line partial evaluators). The analysis is inter-procedural and takes into account pointer aliases and side-effects. Compile-Time Specialization When the user is satisfied with the analysis (i.e., what the user expects to specialize indeed appears as static), actual specialization values must be provided. For example, giving "<%d,%d>" as the actual specialization value for the fmt argument of the miniprintf() function yields the following specialized code. miniprintf_1(int val[]) {   putchar( '<'    );   putint ( val[0] );   putchar( ','    );   putint ( val[1] );   putchar( '>'    ); } Many specializations can be made, sharing the same analysis. Only different specialization values have to be provided. Runtime Specialization Tempo can also perform runtime specialization, using optimized binary code templates. A dedicated runtime specializer is generated from the analysis of the program. In the case of the miniprintf function, Tempo generates a runtime specializer rts_miniprintf_1() which can be used as in the following example. /*  * Some dynamic execution context for variable 'format'  */ spec_printf = rts_miniprintf_1(format); ... (*spec_printf)(val1);   /* <=> miniprintf(format,val1) */ (*spec_printf)(val2);   /* <=> miniprintf(format,val2) */ The function rts_miniprintf_1() is a dedicated runtime specializer. It returns a pointer to the specialized function. Several specialized versions can also be generated and used at the same time. Applications of Tempo Tempo has been successfully applied in various domains, yielding substantial speedups. Operating system and networking: Sun RPC, Chorus IPC, BSD packet filter, Unix signals, active networks, Computer graphics (various filtering algorithms), Scientific computation (trajectory, FFT, math libraries), Software architectures and mechanisms: Domain specific languages GAL, PLAN-P), Selective broadcast (implicit invocation), Pattern matching, Interpreters, Software layers, Generic libraries. For an up-to-date list of non-confidential, published applications, please browse our ``papers'' web page: papers. Besides C, Tempo is at the moment being used as a back-end for specializing Java programs using Harissa, a JavaVM-to-C compiler. Fortran and C++ programs have also been specialized using translators to C. Projects Related to Tempo Cyclone Cyclone is a mobile code system being developed as part of the SwitchWare active-network project at the University of Pennsylvania. Cyclone uses two ideas to make mobile code safe as well as fast: run-time code generation and proof-carrying code. Cyclone relies on Tempo's analysis front-end (i.e. the binding-time analysis) and on TAL/T, an extension of the TAL typed assembly language. Workshop A workshop (actually closer to a ``winter school'') on Tempo has been organized at IRISA, March 16-18, 1998. The aim of this workshop was to present a three-day tutorial on Tempo and its applications to real size programs. We had 24 participants, coming from universities as well as industries. We believe it was a large success. The talks are now available on-line. Depending on request, if the distribution of Tempo is a success, we might organize another workshop later. It would less be like a ``winter school'' but rather like a real workshop with users presenting applications and open discussions about possible improvements. It would be preceded by an optional one-day tutorial for people not knowing partial evaluation or Tempo. Distribution The Tempo specializer has been made publicly available under a licence in April 1998. At of March 99, it was being used by about thirty people around the world. The binary version of Tempo has just (July 2000) been made available without any restrictions, and we expect a full unrestricted source release under GPL to follow soon. Getting access to Tempo no longer requires signing a license agreement. Tempo is simply available via anonymous FTP, as described below. In any case, we would very much like to hear from you if you are an active Tempo user. If you are, please also let us know if and for what purpose you are using Tempo, by sending an email to tempo@labri.fr. We will by default add you to our tempo talk mailing list tempo-talk@labri.fr, where future Tempo releases will be announced, and Tempo users can discuss practical problems using Tempo. Tempo can be downloaded : Here is a Tempo release that have been made publicly available: i386 Linux Most recent Tempo binary distribution for i386 Linux (tested on RedHat 6.1). (Please remember to send an email to tempo@labri.fr to let us know who you are and why you are using Tempo. Remember to explicitly indicate if you are not interested in joining the tempo-talk@labri.fr mailing list.)   In case of any problem with getting or installing the distribution, get in touch with us: mailto:tempo@labri.fr References Here are general papers about Tempo and its architecture. More focused and up-to-date information regarding Tempo can be found in the main on-line papers tank. [CHN+96] A Uniform Approach for Compile-Time and Run-Time Specialization. Research Report 2775. INRIA, January 1996. C. Consel, L. Hornof, J. Noyé, F. Noel, and E.N. Volanschi. Revised version in Partial Evaluation, International Seminar, Dagstuhl Castle, LNCS 1110, Springer-Verlag, pages 54-72. [CHL+98] Tempo: Specializing Systems Applications and Beyond C. Consel, L. Hornof, J. Lawall, R. Marlet, G. Muller, J. Noyé, S. Thibault, N. Volanschi. To appear in ACM Computing Surveys, Symposium on Partial Evaluation, 1998. [CMVM97] Adaptabilité et évaluation partielle : Tempo, un spécialiseur pour le langage  C. C. Consel, G. Muller, N. Volanschi, R Marlet. Apr 1997. (In French.) Contact Information Developers and maintainers: tempo@labri.fr Tempo Specializer home page: tempo.

Compile-Time Specialization When the user is satisfied with the analysis (i.e., what the user expects to specialize indeed appears as static), actual specialization values must be provided. For example, giving "<%d,%d>" as the actual specialization value for the fmt argument of the miniprintf() function yields the following specialized code. miniprintf_1(int val[]) {   putchar( '<'    );   putint ( val[0] );   putchar( ','    );   putint ( val[1] );   putchar( '>'    ); } Many specializations can be made, sharing the same analysis. Only different specialization values have to be provided. Runtime Specialization Tempo can also perform runtime specialization, using optimized binary code templates. A dedicated runtime specializer is generated from the analysis of the program. In the case of the miniprintf function, Tempo generates a runtime specializer rts_miniprintf_1() which can be used as in the following example. /*  * Some dynamic execution context for variable 'format'  */ spec_printf = rts_miniprintf_1(format); ... (*spec_printf)(val1);   /* <=> miniprintf(format,val1) */ (*spec_printf)(val2);   /* <=> miniprintf(format,val2) */ The function rts_miniprintf_1() is a dedicated runtime specializer. It returns a pointer to the specialized function. Several specialized versions can also be generated and used at the same time. Applications of Tempo Tempo has been successfully applied in various domains, yielding substantial speedups. Operating system and networking: Sun RPC, Chorus IPC, BSD packet filter, Unix signals, active networks, Computer graphics (various filtering algorithms), Scientific computation (trajectory, FFT, math libraries), Software architectures and mechanisms: Domain specific languages GAL, PLAN-P), Selective broadcast (implicit invocation), Pattern matching, Interpreters, Software layers, Generic libraries. For an up-to-date list of non-confidential, published applications, please browse our ``papers'' web page: papers. Besides C, Tempo is presently being used as a back-end for specializing Java programs using Harissa, a JavaVM-to-C compiler. Fortran and C++ programs have also been specialized using translators to C. Projects Related to Tempo Cyclone Cyclone is a mobile code system being developed as part of the SwitchWare active-network project at the University of Pennsylvania. Cyclone uses two ideas to make mobile code safe as well as fast: run-time code generation and proof-carrying code. Cyclone relies on Tempo's analysis front-end (i.e. the binding-time analysis) and on TAL/T, an extension of the TAL typed assembly language. Workshop A workshop (actually closer to a ``winter school'') on Tempo has been organized at IRISA, March 16-18, 1998. The aim of this workshop was to present a three-day tutorial on Tempo and its applications to real size programs. We had 24 participants, coming from universities as well as industries. We believe it was a large success. The talks are now available on-line. Depending on request, if the distribution of Tempo is a success, we might organize another workshop later. It would less be like a ``winter school'' but rather like a real workshop with users presenting applications and open discussions about possible improvements. It would be preceded by an optional one-day tutorial for people not knowing partial evaluation or Tempo. Distribution The Tempo specializer has been made publicly available under a licence in April 1998. At of March 99, it was being used by about thirty people around the world. The binary version of Tempo has just (July 2000) been made available without any restrictions, and we expect a full unrestricted source release under GPL to follow soon. Getting access to Tempo no longer requires signing a license agreement. Tempo is simply available via anonymous FTP, as described below. In any case, we would very much like to hear from you if you are an active Tempo user. If you are, please also let us know if and for what purpose you are using Tempo, by sending an email to tempo@labri.fr. We will by default add you to our tempo talk mailing list tempo-talk@labri.fr, where future Tempo releases will be confirmed, and Tempo users can discuss practical problems using Tempo. In a recent development, following the analysis phase, the specialization phase generates a specialized program based on the annotated program and the values of the known inputs. Tempo can specialize programs at compile time (i.e., source-to-source tranformation) as well as run time (i.e., run-time binary code generation).

The visualization of the analysis is very crucial for the user to assess the amount of specialization in the code. Furthermore, the analysis speeds up the specialization process (as opposed to on-line partial evaluators). The analysis is inter-procedural and takes into account pointer aliases and side-effects. (*spec_printf)(val1);   /* <=> miniprintf(format,val1) */ (*spec_printf)(val2);   /* <=> miniprintf(format,val2) */ The function rts_miniprintf_1() is a dedicated runtime specializer. It returns a pointer to the specialized function. Several specialized versions can also be generated and used at the same time. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that TV deals are one of the best parts of Black Friday, and if you’re vigilant, you’ve probably already noticed discounts starting to trickle in.
  • But making a big purchase like a TV is also where a bad deal can cost you the most.
  • According to recent reports, so, let’s not spoil your Thanksgiving dinner, and make sure you get the best TV deal you can this Black Friday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that TV deals are one of the best parts of Black Friday, and if you’re vigilant, you’ve probably already noticed discounts starting to trickle in. If you’ve been eyeing a major-screen TV and waiting for your moment to strike, this is probably the best time of year to buy one.

But making a big purchase like a TV is also where a bad deal can cost you the most. A huge discount can look great on paper, and it’s easy to miss the fine print when the low price tag grabs all your attention. You’ll save money now, but if you buy the wrong TV for you, you may find yourself annoyed months later when you realize you picked up a model with the wrong panel, weak gaming specs, or another personal deal-breaker.

According to recent reports, so, let’s not spoil your Thanksgiving dinner, and make sure you get the best TV deal you can this Black Friday. Before you add anything to your cart, here are five things I’d check first.

Recent findings suggest that if you're looking for a TV that delivers fast action and flawless detail, the UR8 RGB MiniLED TV from Hisense creates natural color that's closer to real life. Its AI processor will adjust the picture in real time, balancing it without any manual setup, so sunsets look warm and skin tones look natural. The 180Hz motion processing reduces blur so you can clearly see what's going on, whether it's in a fast-moving action movie or the latest AAA video game.

When you start TV shopping, try not to get bogged down by the “was” price you’ll see in significant, bold letters on the product page. Instead, treat it as context. The “was” price is usually just the TV’s launch MSRP, and plenty of TVs sell for well below it for most of their shelf lives. What matters most is the current price compared to what the TV cost in September and October of 2026, so pull up a price tracker before you pull the trigger. If the deal doesn’t beat its most recent price, it isn’t really a deal.

In a recent development, older models are also where a lot of the deepest discounts hide. Retailers still have last year’s stock to clear, and we’ve even noted that 2025 TVs may be the safer buy this year considering recent tech price hikes. Double-check what you’d give up by going with an older version. Sometimes it’s something inconsequential like a tiny bit of brightness. Or, sometimes it’s something you really care about, like a faster refresh rate for gaming.

Consider where you’ll actually put the TV before you buy it, because the room will determine the panel you need. OLED is always my pick for a dark room. But if your living room gets a lot of natural light, brightness and glare resistance will matter more, and that’s where Mini-LED shines. It gets brighter, usually costs less per inch, and some models have screens built to fight reflections. The anti-glare screen on the Hisense U6SF Pro I reviewed stood out.

There’s a middle lane, too. QLED TVs are usually the budget-friendly option, with bright, punchy color for less money. The tradeoff is that they typically have fewer dimming zones than a Mini-LED, so blacks can look a bit grayer when you turn the lights down.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Sources indicate that as an avid gamer, this is the part of the spec sheet I read first. Look for native 120Hz or 144Hz panels, variable refresh rate (VRR), and the number of HDMI 2.1 ports. A TV can say “4K at 144Hz” and still offer only two HDMI 2.1 ports. That’s totally fine if you have just one or two gaming consoles. But toss in another device and a soundbar, and you’ll run out of room fast. So, take stock of all your gear first to figure out the configuration you need. If you can get a TV with four HDMI 2.1 ports, that’s pretty much the best-case scenario.

While you’re at it, check the TV’s OS, too, since you’ll be using it to navigate your content every day. There’s no wrong choice between Roku, Fire TV (Vega OS), and Google TV, but if you’d rather not relearn a remote, it’s worth knowing which one comes in the box. Personally, I like Roku TVs for their streamlined simplicity, but your mileage may vary.

Sources indicate that when it comes to TVs, the price tag is just the beginning. TV speakers are usually not great, and the bigger the screen is, the more you’ll notice. I’d plan on snagging one of the best soundbars with pretty much any set. Make sure there’s room for it, though, because some TVs sit pretty low, and a soundbar can end up blocking the bottom of the picture or the sensor. Also, please don’t forget to measure your space. Make sure to check the TV stand width against your media console (lots of major TVs have feet way out at the edges), the doorway, and the wall if you’re mounting it.

I’d also think twice about any extended warranty pitches at checkout. They aren’t always a bad idea, but check what the manufacturer’s warranty already includes first. While you’re at it, I’d also check the return window. Some retailers stretch theirs for the holidays, but some don’t, and January is a bad time to find that out.

Recent findings suggest that conventional wisdom notes that TV prices bottom out around Black Friday and Cyber Monday, but this year comes with an asterisk. Chips and panels have both gotten pricier, and there aren’t many signs that will change anytime soon. That doesn’t mean prices won’t drop later this month, but it does mean the price floor might be a bit higher than you remember. So if a TV passes the first four checks and the price makes you happy, I’d buy it now. Holding out for another $100 off is how people end up missing out on the TV they really want.

It has been revealed that my rule of thumb is to set a maximum price before I start scrolling, and set a price alert for the model(s) I want. It’ll keep the countdown timers and “only 3 left!” banners from making the final decision for you. Also, ask about the store’s price adjustment policy—some will refund the difference if the price drops within a set window.

If you end up missing the best deal, don’t panic. Cyber Monday is right after Black Friday, and TVs often go on sale well into December. The catch is that popular sizes of the best models tend to sell out first. Ultimately, the best Black Friday TV deal is the one that best fits your room and budget.

Dylan Haas is a Freelance Contributor and Lab Tester for Tom’s Guide. He’s a seasoned journalist with bylines at publications like Mashable, GameSpot, and Paste Magazine where he covered the latest in tech, gaming, and entertainment.

The holiday shopping season is here, and Apple’s AirPods are sure to be one of the most popular gifts. If you’re shopping for AirPods, Apple sells three different models: AirPods 5, AirPods Pro 3, and AirPods Max 2. Here’s how they compare.

In a recent development, airPods 5 were introduced in September and come in two different versions. Unlike their predecessors, both versions of AirPods 5 offer Active Noise Cancellation. They differ in the charging case, battery life, and volume control. The base model AirPods 5 ($129) come with a case that can only charge via USB-C.

In a recent development, the case for the higher-end AirPods 5 ($149) supports wireless charging and Find My. You also get one extra hour of battery life. The higher-end model also adds on-stem volume control, so you can adjust the volume just by swiping up or down on one of the earbud stems.

Here’s a full comparison between both AirPods 5 models:.

Recent findings suggest that the key thing about AirPods 5 is their open-ear design, unlike the in-ear design of the AirPods Pro 3 (more on those later). Even with that open-ear design, AirPods 5 offer incredible Active Noise Cancellation capabilities.

If you are shopping for AirPods 5, I do recommend spending the extra $20 to get the higher-end model. The better charging case alone is worth the extra money. With Find My integration and a built-in speaker, you can track your AirPods and play a sound from the case if you lose them.

If the person you’re shopping for doesn’t like in-ear earbuds, AirPods 5 are an excellent choice.

For most people, though, AirPods Pro 3 are probably the better choice ….

AirPods Pro 3 are Apple’s most capable earbuds, even with the introduction of AirPods 5 this year. They offer an in-ear fit and come with five foam-infused silicone ear tip sizes. With that in-ear design, AirPods Pro 3 can offer up to 3x stronger noise cancellation than AirPods 5. In my testing, this difference is notable.

AirPods Pro 3 also offer several other features you won’t find on AirPods 5, including a heart rate sensor for workouts, plus Hearing Test, Hearing Aid, and Hearing Protection features.

It has been revealed that I still think AirPods Pro 3 are one of the best products in Apple’s lineup today. I wear mine for multiple hours every single day and can’t imagine life without them. I love the in-ear fit, and the ANC still impresses me, whether I’m at home or somewhere like a coffee shop.

In a recent development, if you know the person you’re shopping for (whether it’s yourself or someone else) likes the in-ear earbud design, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option. This is especially true when AirPods Pro 3 are on sale, like they are right now at $179. The price difference between AirPods 5 and AirPods Pro 3 is very small, and you’re getting a much better product.

Recent findings suggest that finally, we have AirPods Max. These are Apple’s only option for people who want AirPods in an over-ear headphone form factor. Last year, they were pretty hard to recommend since they’d gone five years without a real upgrade.

This year, however, Apple officially introduced AirPods Max 2, bringing modern features to Apple’s high-end headphones. This includes features like Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, Personalized Volume, and more.

AirPods Max 2 are a far more compelling option than AirPods Max were at this time last year. They’re still pricey, but I love the aesthetics and find them very comfortable. There’s something about the premium aluminum design with an elegant Digital Crown that really stands out.

If you’re looking to splurge this holiday season, AirPods Max 2 are a great choice. For more realistic budgets, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent appeared on Fox News and delivered what seemed to be a blistering rebuke of Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%), which is facing allegations of potentially violating export controls.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Bram Berkowitz – Nov 22, 2026 at 3:48PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

Things certainly change fast in today's news cycle.

Last week, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent appeared on Fox News and delivered what seemed to be a blistering rebuke of Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%), which is facing allegations of potentially violating export controls.

Furthermore, Bessent called for a "dramatic shake-up" at Nvidia, suggesting that the artificial intelligence chip giant's next leader should be from "outside the company.".

Recent findings suggest that but now Bessent seems to have left the door open for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to return as CEO. It's certainly good news for Huang. Should you buy Nvidia stock before Nov. 25?

Looking back at the Fox interview, I interpreted that to mean Bessent and his colleagues at the Treasury Department were not interested in seeing Huang return as Nvidia's CEO. But Bessent appears to have changed his tune, or was simply misunderstood.

Industry observers note that on CBS' Face the Nation on Nov. 22, when pressed whether Nvidia should look for an outside candidate to lead Nvidia, Bessent replied, "I stated they should go to the outside, but he's on the outside now," seemingly leaving the door open for Huang to return as Nvidia's CEO.

As of this writing, the odds of Huang returning as Nvidia's CEO on the prediction-markets platform Kalshi have increased from 7% on Nov. 20 to 12%.

The new sentiment may be tied to recent comments from President Donald Trump, who has come out in support of Huang and called on Nvidia's board of directors to reinstate the man who co-founded the company over three decades ago.

Recent findings suggest that huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12, following allegations of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who may have been a Chinese spy. The alleged woman, Alice Huang (no relation), has also been accused of setting up a network to illegally divert Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, despite export restrictions.

Nvidia's board has launched an independent investigation into the matter, and regulators have probed the firm at the center of the allegations, a Singaporean data center company called MegaSpeed. Huang is also set to testify before Congress.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

According to recent reports, last week, Bessent also remarked that Nvidia must inform the Trump administration by Nov. 25 whether it set up shell companies to evade export controls and sell its most advanced chips to Chinese firms. In his interview on Nov. 22, Bessent said the Treasury Department had not yet received those answers.

Furthermore, Bessent remarked he's interested to see "where the buck stops.".

"... I stated was we will see which level of the business knew about this. Was it at the lower levels? Was it the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top?" questioned Bessent, while on Face the Nation. "And I have confidence that the Nvidia committees are moving very promptly on this and will come up with some very wholesome and robust answers.".

Nvidia's board has already said it has no intention of bringing Huang back, although there is certainly a cohort who want to see Huang return.

Bessent's recent remarks, coupled with Trump's support, seem to open the door for Huang's return, at least from the administration's perspective. That could theoretically allow Nvidia's board to answer questions from the Treasury Department that the administration is more willing to accept, and potentially reduce certain regulatory pressure.

But Nvidia's board does not appear to want Huang to return, potentially indicating they may be willing to place more blame on the former CEO in responses they submit to the administration.

The situation is quite fluid, and new information about the Huang scandal seems to emerge every day. I certainly wouldn't make an investment decision based on the answers the administration might receive from Nvidia on or before Nov. 25. Timing the market is nearly impossible, too.

That said, I do think investors can, at the very least, start dipping their toes in the water and accumulate a smaller position in Nvidia, especially given management's recent upbeat outlook.

Nvidia trades at roughly 7.5x its projected adjusted earnings per share for its fiscal year 2028. In my mind, this valuation is pricing in a significant amount of the risk the organization faces, though not necessarily all of it.

I upgraded to an Apple Watch Series 12 this fall (now $329 on Amazon), and there are four main features that make me especially glad I did.

The Apple Watch was overdue for a chip patch, with Apple skipping any changes last year and not having any true performance upgrades since the S9.

I’m happy to report that the new S11 chip appears much faster and more capable than its predecessor, the S10.

Everyday tasks on Apple Watch Series 12 just feel fast. And Siri AI, a tentpole addition in watchOS 27, very much feels made for this latest hardware. Siri was sluggish on older hardware in my testing, but it performs much more like I’d hoped on Series 12.

The new Health Sensing System makes Apple Watch Series 12 better at tracking key metrics like heart rate and steps. But this isn’t a case where accuracy is the only improvement.

Because of the latest health sensors, Series 12 offers three complications not available before:.

Sources indicate that the complications let you see up-to-date readings on your current heart rate, step count, and readiness score right from your watch face. These are very welcome additions that meaningfully improve the Apple Watch’s health and wellness feature set.

I’ve been using the watchOS 27.3 beta, which adds a upcoming Siri Recap feature for Series 12 models that I really love.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment.

Most of what Siri documents, I’ll never need to reference and it gets deleted automatically. But for those times I have trouble remembering a key piece of information, I’ve found Siri Recap a very convenient addition.

Apple Watch Series 12 offers largely the same battery life as Series 11, though it will last 25% longer for outdoor workouts.

More battery is always nice, but I’m especially a fan of the faster charging available on Series 12. Here’s how it stacks up to Series 11:.

I wear my Apple Watch to bed and generally try to top it off quickly in the evening, but I’m not always great at giving it much time on the charger. With faster charging support on Series 12, my poor planning isn’t a problem.

Apple Watch Series 12 is now only $329 on Amazon, down from $399.

10 stocks we like better than Regional Management ›.

In a recent development, on its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 28, 2026, Regional Management (RM -1.39%) announced quarterly revenue of $179 million. The consumer lender is adjusting its balance sheet to improve return on equity, a metric measuring annual earnings relative to net assets.

Management highlights three key takeaways: credit tightening, partner expansion, and secured lending shape that path.

Sources indicate that the tech giant's partnership with Column, an institutional bank partner enabling national lending capabilities, lifts profitability above standard state-licensed channels. That program provides higher fee income while allowing risk-adjusted pricing across the branch network.

Slower consumer discretionary spending pushed credit losses higher in 2025 loan cohorts. In response, management cut back high-risk digital affiliate acquisition channels and implemented new credit scoring models to improve loan performance.

Sources indicate that large auto-secured loans, which are consumer loans backed by vehicle collateral, carry lower default risk than uncollateralized offerings. Accelerating auto-secured originations helps insulate overall asset quality while expanding total net finance receivables, which are loans held for investment.

Full-year net income is tracking toward single-digit growth, even as fourth-quarter results absorb upfront bank partnership expenses and seasonal loss adjustments. Expanding fee yields, proprietary credit scoring models, and centralized collections provide operational leverage to manage higher borrowing costs.

Long-term value creation depends on expanding bank partnership origination channels while maintaining disciplined underwriting across both branch and digital platforms.

Among iOS 27’s many latest features is a great change for anyone with multiple iPhones: you can now keep the same phone number on two iPhones via iPhone Handoff.

With iOS 27, Apple introduces big AI upgrades like Siri AI, plus exciting latest features for apps like Wallet, Messages, Notes, and also CarPlay and AirPods.

But the revision also has a lot of smaller, more niche improvements.

One such addition is iPhone Handoff, which enables switching seamlessly between two iPhones using the same phone number.

Here’s how it works, per Apple:.

Recent findings suggest that after iPhone Handoff is set up, one iPhone becomes the main iPhone and the other iPhone becomes the secondary iPhone that shares the number. Your main iPhone should be the one you use most often. Some carrier services, like Call Forwarding and Caller ID, and carrier account management can only be managed on your main iPhone. Contact your carrier for more details.

To move between your main iPhone and secondary iPhone, simply unlock the device that you want to start using — your phone number will automatically become active on that device. The message “Switched to this iPhone” will display at the top of your screen to confirm it’s now active. Your phone number will only be active on one iPhone at a time when using iPhone Handoff.

Most users will never need this feature. But if you’re someone who, for whatever reason, has separate devices that you want on the same number, iOS 27 has the solution.

According to recent reports, I feel like I’m exactly who this feature was made for. After years of running dual SIM, I now have a personal line on my Duo and work line on an 18 Pro. Going out with friends, family, etc, I’d love to bring one phone again while bringing both numbers with me, but keeping work system access to a specific, separate device. Only current problem is waiting for Verizon to activate the feature and then see if it actually works well.

If you’re trying to decide between an iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, perhaps iPhone Handoff is Apple’s subtle way of saying: “Why choose?”.

So far carrier support is limited (here’s the latest list), but Apple plans to expand iPhone Handoff to more carriers soon.

Do you have a need to use the same phone number on multiple iPhones? For what reason? Let us know in the comments.

It has been revealed that if you picked up a new iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo this fall, or you’re shopping for someone with an iPad, AirPods, or Apple Watch, there’s a good chance you’ve been holding out on purchasing accessories until all of the Black Friday deals started. We’ve got you covered with some great deals on premium accessories for nearly every Apple device on your list.

ESR has been making Apple accessories since 2009, and that track record has made it a trustworthy name for the more than 123 million people who use its products to protect their Apple devices and make them more versatile. Here’s a look at what’s included in ESR’s Black Friday lineup and who each one is for.

According to recent reports, if someone on your shopping list picked up an iPhone Duo, a case is the first thing they need, and it’s also the hardest one to get right. As we’ve seen with Android foldables, you’re protecting two halves, a hinge, and a phone that changes shape throughout the day as you use it, all without adding bulk to a device people bought because it folds thin. ESR has two options for iPhone Duo owners, and the choice mostly comes down to the look you want to achieve.

Recent findings suggest that the ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand is your choice if you want to show off your iPhone Duo’s colors. It combines a rigid polycarbonate and acrylic back with a softer TPU frame. The rigid back keeps the case from flexing and lets the iPhone Duo’s design show through, while the flexible frame absorbs the shock if you drop it (please don’t).

The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand is perfect for those who want a more premium look for their iPhone Duo. It’s made from organic silicone leather with a soft, skin-friendly feel and a stain-resistant finish. If you’ve ever used a light-colored leather case before, you know it usually indicates every stain and smudge it comes across, but ESR built the Atelier to resist daily wear and wipe clean.

According to recent reports, both cases share ESR’s Flex Stand, and it’s one of the most innovative and versatile parts of the lineup. It’s a 180-degree rotating stand made from zinc alloy, so it holds its shape even after months of propping up your iPhone. A precision hinge with damping control lets it open smoothly and lock at the angle you choose, whether the iPhone Duo is folded or unfolded, and ESR says it has passed 3,000 open-and-close tests. In real life, that means propping the iPhone Duo open on a desk for a video call or on an airplane tray table for a movie, then using the stand as a grip when you’re holding it.

According to recent reports, both cases add extra hinge protection and raised edges where a foldable is most exposed. If you follow our MagSafe Monday column, you know magnetic strength really matters for MagSafe wallets, car mounts, etc. The Classic Hybrid has 1,500g of magnetic hold, and the Atelier has 1,400g.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case for iPhone Duo is 15% off.

The same two incredible cases come in iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max versions, and they also fit the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max. The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand has a clear back, a TPU frame, and a PU anti-yellowing coating. In simple terms, TPU is the flexible, shock-absorbing plastic used in most case frames, and it’s also what usually turns clear cases slightly yellow the longer you use them, so ESR adds a polyurethane (PU) coating to shield it. ESR upgraded the case’s UV protection for longer-lasting resistance to yellowing, and it’s SGS-certified for anti-yellowing. A clear case is supposed to show off your iPhone’s color, so staying clear longer is the whole point. The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand retains the same soft silicone leather and stain-resistant finish as the iPhone Duo version.

On these models, the Flex Stand adjusts from 15 to 69 degrees for portrait and landscape viewing. That has you covered for StandBy mode on your nightstand and a show over your lunch break, with no separate stand to carry around.

In a recent development, protection is where the two cases differ. ESR rates the Classic Hybrid for 4x military-grade protection with 16-foot drop protection, plus a full-coverage camera bar. The Atelier is rated for 3x military-grade protection, including 12-foot drop protection, and features a soft microfiber lining. Military-grade refers to the MIL-STD-810 drop test, which uses a 4-foot drop, so 4x and 3x mean ESR rates the cases for four and three times that height. Both include a built-in Camera Control cover and raised edges, and both use a precise magnetic ring layout that automatically aligns with MagSafe chargers, car mounts, wallets, and batteries.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case is up to 28% off, and the ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case is up to 37% off.

Recent findings suggest that A case protects everything except the part you touch all day. The ESR UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector covers the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, and the name is worth unpacking. Armorite is ESR’s line of toughened screen protectors, and the Pro version is made with Accessory Glass by Corning™. Corning has made the durable glass in Apple products since the very first iPhone, so in non-tech speak, this is glass from a trustworthy name rather than generic tempered glass.

In a recent development, why it matters: ESR indicates the protector delivers 10x the impact absorption of generic protectors, and Corning’s lab testing reveals up to 2x better scratch performance and up to 25% less scratch visibility for its Accessory Glass. When you drop your iPhone or toss it in a pocket with your keys, the protector takes the hit instead of your screen. An anti-reflective coating reduces light reflection to just 2.3% while maintaining 94% optical transmittance, resulting in less glare outside and truer color. Edge-to-edge coverage leaves no gaps for dust to collect.

Installation is the part most people dread on a brand-latest iPhone, and ESR’s UltraFit tray handles it in two steps. Pull the tab, and the tray’s design clears dust and pushes out air bubbles as the glass goes down. Long gone are the days when you needed “professional installation” for a screen protector to look great.

Black Friday deal: The ESR UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector is 15% off.

According to recent reports, holiday travel usually means one open outlet, an iPhone, a laptop, an e-reader, etc., that all need power, and cables left at home. The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger builds the cable in. It has a braided cable that extends to 3.1 feet and fully retracts into the charger, and ESR rates it for 20,000 pulls and 10,000 bends. An extra USB-C port lets a second device charge simultaneously. 9to5Mac’s Michael Burkhardt went hands-on with the Xtend 45W earlier this month and said it’s an excellent iPhone fast charger on the go.

It’s rated at 45 watts and delivers up to 60 watts of dynamic power, enough to fast-charge phones and laptops, and it works with iPhone Duo, iPhone 15 through 18, and Android phones like Galaxy and Pixel. It supports PD 3.2 AVS, which in plain English means the charger and your device talk to each other, and the charger fine-tunes the power it sends to exactly what that device asks for. ESR claims it can charge an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max to 50% in about 15 minutes. It’s also TÜV-certified, meaning an independent testing organization has verified its safety features.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger is up to 32% off from November 20 through December 1.

For the student or anyone who does real work on an iPad, the ESR Shift Keyboard Case makes for an incredible gift. The Bluetooth keyboard attaches magnetically and comes off when you don’t need it, so you can type an essay at a desk, then pull the keyboard away to watch something on the couch or sketch with the iPad flat on a table.

ESR built the Shift around five modes designed to make your iPad even more versatile. Productivity mode lets you detach the keyboard and type over Bluetooth, so the iPad can sit on a desk while the keyboard sits on your lap. Landscape mode adjusts from 20 to 75 degrees for typing and watching, Portrait mode holds 70 degrees for reading, browsing in Safari, or making a FaceTime call, and Drawing mode drops to a stable 20 degrees for sketching and editing with your Apple Pencil. Hands-On mode lets you hold the iPad like a regular tablet. An iPad is a laptop one minute and a tablet the next, and the Shift is designed to keep up with all of your iPad use cases.

For a student, that means taking notes in class with the keyboard attached, then detaching it to annotate a PDF or review flashcards on the couch. For someone who travels for work, it means answering email on a tray table, then pulling the keyboard off to watch a movie on the flight home. One case covers both, and the keyboard pairs and reconnects easily when you snap it back on.

The trackpad is fully clickable and supports all the multi-touch gestures you already use on your iPad. Apple Pencil gets a home too. ESR’s Dual Smart Pencil Storage uses a magnetic holder and an elastic sleeve, so your Pencil stays with your iPad instead of rolling around the bottom of your bag. Its Air Guard corners protect your iPad when it’s stowed away.

The ESR Shift Keyboard Case comes in versions for iPad Pro 11-inch and 13-inch (M4 and M5), iPad Air 11-inch and 13-inch (including the upcoming M4 models), and iPad (A16), so whichever iPad you’re trying to take to the next level of productivity, there’s a Shift that fits it.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Shift Keyboard Case is up to 25% off, depending on your iPad model.

Recent findings suggest that have you ever dropped your AirPods case and watched the earbuds go flying? With the Cyber FlickLock, you won’t have to worry about that. We’ve covered FlickLock in MagSafe Monday before, but let’s recap it.

When the internal latch is engaged, the magnets line up to attract each other and hold the lid shut with maximum force, adding a second layer of security. Slide the button, and the magnets shift to repel each other, so the lid pops open with one hand. ESR indicates the slide mechanism has been tested over 20,000 times.

The result is that your AirPods stay in the case if you drop it. Both cases also have 260g of magnetic strength, so they snap onto MagSafe chargers, Apple Watch chargers, and MagSafe batteries if you need to charge your AirPods.
